title: ‘Northbound’ Review: Bruce Dern Revs Up a Road Movie With Its Hands Otherwise Firmly at Ten and Two
description: There is a pleasantly peppery performance from a bewhiskered — and bewhiskyed — Bruce Dern in William Scoular’s “Northbound,” but its spice is lost
body:
There is a pleasantly peppery performance from a bewhiskered — and bewhiskyed — Bruce Dern in William Scoular’s “Northbound,” but its spice is lost to the coziness of an approach that sets a higher premium on amiability than originality. Kicking off to Trooper’s stadium staple “Raise a Little Hell” and closing out with the plaintive piano-rock of Keane’s “Somewhere Only We Know,” in between, “Northbound” plots such a straight line from one mood to the other, from mildly irascible rebellion to melodic, melancholic wisdom, that its central road trip feels less like a late-life adventure and more like a familiar commute. But the time of its overly neat wrap-up, the only unanswered question here is why we needed so many large-print signposts for an emotional journey that never leaves the well-trafficked highway. 
	

	Dern, echoing his Oscar-nominated “Nebraska” role just with the edges sanded down, plays Arthur, an octogenarian hellion who demonstrates his refusal to go gentle into that good night by careening around the manicured lawns of his elder-care home in a golf cart, accompanied by a sex worker and a bottle of tequila. Duly, he is expelled from the place, and is picked up resignedly by his grandson, Kevin (Hunter Parrish). Kevin has been given brusque instructions by his distant businessman father (Dylan Baker) to put Arthur on a plane bound for the next in a long line of nursing facilities. Arthur has other ideas.


	Chiefly, he is hankering to go home — by which he means back to Canada, to the ex-wife (Joanna Cassidy) he claims still to love, and to the small-batch whisky distillery he founded decades before. Fueled by affection for Gramps, by nostalgia for a childhood steeped in whiskymaking lore, and by a distinct lack of zeal for his law-firm day job, Kevin agrees to drive him the 2,000-odd miles from Arizona. Some intergenerational sparring ensues, as Kevin scolds Arthur for his more outré boomer comments, and Arthur in turn sneers at his grandson’s millennial lameness. Urging the younger man to be more romantically proactive, at one point Arthur invokes Lancelot and Guinevere. “Nobody cares about that macho shit, Gramps,” sniffs Kevin piously, as he moisturizes before bedtime. “The Round Table was nothing but a circle-jerk of toxic masculinity.”
	

	Thankfully, just as Ashlin Halfnight’s pro forma screenplay begins to chug on the fumes of old-chestnut gags about how uptight Kevin is and how long it takes Arthur to pee, they pick up Adrien (Julia Fox), a pretty, deaf hitchhiker and things get a bit more lively, as they tend to do whenever Julia Fox is involved. She turns out to be neither deaf, nor an errant claims processor on her way to Buffalo; instead her real backstory means not only can she handle herself in a fight, she actually has quite an urgent reason for needing to cross the border. It is also, unfortunately, a story that deserves a more serious-minded drama than “Northbound” wants to be, and its cursory treatment here is one of the film’s frustrations. 

	But as Peter Menzies Jr.’s attractive cinematography segues into another drone shot drifting over a winding road or a forested lakeside, and another obvious needle-drop reminds anyone who may be looking away from the screen that we’re “Back on the Road” again or that someone is hurting someone they love to “You Always Hurt the One You Love,” it becomes apparent that the movie suffers from misplaced focus in general. Its fine supporting cast (including Baker, Fox, Cassidy and the late Graham Greene in a too-brief cameo) is sidelined by a script that keeps insisting the least interesting character is the most important. No shade on Parrish — as written, milquetoast Kevin is little more than an air of genial befuddlement with a jawline, an impression not helped by the predictability of his arc. His main dilemma — whether to veto the sale of the underperforming distillery and run it himself, or return Stateside to a job and a life he clearly dislikes — is hardly a Scylla-or-Charibdis situation.

	Despite his top billing and his undeniable curmudgeon charisma, even Dern ends up underserved by a role that is eventually reduced to so much benign backdrop for a much blander hero’s journey. There can be no doubting the sincerity of Scoular’s ambition to pay admiring tribute to a larger-than-life elder, but like too many portrayals of seniors, this one stops short of imagining that the life experience of an older person might have intrinsic, first-person value, rather than being solely of instructional usefulness to a younger generation who can parse it for inspirational or cautionary motivation. In so doing, the terminally nice “Northbound” goes south, squandering its greatest asset by all but giving him a halo when surely, a guy like Arthur would have more than a little hell left to raise.

schema.headline: ‘Northbound’ Review: Bruce Dern Revs Up a Road Movie With Its Hands Otherwise Firmly at Ten and Two

title: Ewan McGregor Says Next Obi-Wan Kenobi Project Could Be Tracking Down Yoda or a ‘Big Love Story’ With Wife Mary Elizabeth Winstead’s ‘Ahsoka’ Character: ‘There’s Got to Be Something’
description: Ewan McGregor has recently been very vocal about his desire to return as Obi-Wan Kenobi — and even has a few pitches for what his “Star Wars” charac
body:
Ewan McGregor has recently been very vocal about his desire to return as Obi-Wan Kenobi — and even has a few pitches for what his “Star Wars” character could get up to in a new project.

	Speaking at the Variety Lounge at Edinburgh International Film Festival, the Scottish star said he’d got as far as taking his ideas to Lucasfilm boss Dave Filoni, who was shooting “Ahsoka” with his wife Mary Elizabeth Winstead at the time.
	

	“It was very casual, but I said there’s got to be something,” McGregor said. “Because Yoda’s somewhere else. After the end of ‘Episode III’, when we all go to the four or five corners of the galaxy — or however many corners it’s got! — I won’t have been in touch with him. But he’s out there. So I think there could be a story there where I’m trying to reach out to him.”

	Speaking of “Ahsoka,” when Winstead joined the series as New Republic general Hera Syndulla, McGregor said he also began dreaming up ideas for Kenobi.

	“I got very excited when Mary started working on ‘Ahsoka’. I thought, maybe this is the big love story — Obi-Wan and Hera,” he said. However, while McGregor said that “time doesn’t really mean anything” in the various “multiverses” of Star Wars, he acknowledged that Kenobi and Hera “were in different time frames.”

	Whether McGregor gets to don the Jedi master’s trademark robes again remains to be seen (Filoni very recently told Variety on the D23 red carpet that “The Hunt for Ben Solo” movie was currently not in the works), but he reiterated that he’d “be up” for returning in any feature or series. “I enjoyed doing the series very much… and would be happy to do it again. I like playing him — he’s a really good character to play.”
	

	Away from galaxies far far away and to somewhere much closer to home, McGregor also discussed with Variety how much he enjoyed moving back to Scotland and his home region of Perthshire.

	“It feel really, really good — I’m surprised how effortless it’s been,” he said. “I didn’t imagine it, but I’m really glad of it — I feel very comfortable there. And I’ve got my little boy, who’s 5, and he’s going to grow up there in much the same way that I did, which is nice.”

	He added that he’s been enjoying jumping on his Vespa to meet family members, including his brother in the north of Scotland.

	“I just went up there for a cup of tea with him,” he said. “And when I got back, I realized I’d never had that experience in my whole adult life, of being able to pop round. I’ve always lived somewhere. I left home at 16. I was really missing something all these years, but now I can jump on my bike and I’ll be at my mum and dad’s house in half an hour.”

	As well as living up in Perthshire, McGregor has also found work there, recently announced as joining Alan Cumming next year in an stage adaptation of Harry Macqueen’s acclaimed feature “Supernova” at the Pitlochry Festival Theatre.

	“We’ve done two readings of it, just of the film script,” he said. “But I’ve never got through the read-throughs without bawling my eyes out — it’s just so moving.”

schema.headline: Ewan McGregor Says Next Obi-Wan Kenobi Project Could Be Tracking Down Yoda or a ‘Big Love Story’ With Wife Mary Elizabeth Winstead’s ‘Ahsoka’ Character: ‘There’s Got to Be Something’

title: Producers Scout for K-pop Talent With U.S. Appeal During KCON Fan Festival in Los Angeles
description: In a makeshift audition booth assembled in a far corner on the ground floor of the Los Angeles Convention Center, a steady stream of K-pop lovers to
body:
In a makeshift audition booth assembled in a far corner on the ground floor of the Los Angeles Convention Center, a steady stream of K-pop lovers took their shot this past weekend.

	As part of the annual KCON Korean entertainment and culture festival, producers of a hit Korean talent competition series held auditions on Aug. 14-15 for the upcoming season of “Girls Planet,” a making-of-the-band story in which viewers will vote on the members of a new all-female K-pop group.
	

	Veteran South Korean TV producer Kim Sinyoung is chief producer of “Girls Planet 2027” and the previous three seasons of the “Planet” competition series. He was on hand at KCON in downtown L.A. to keep an eye on the turnout for the open-audition opportunity at the three-day event produced by CJ ENM, the same company that produces “Girls Planet” and also owns Mnet, the South Korean network on which it originates.


	The stakes are high for Season 4 as Mnet has partnered with music industry powerhouse Republic Collective to bring a twist to the competition series. This time around the focus will be on assembling a K-pop group designed to appeal to U.S. and Western audiences. Republic is home to many of the biggest acts in contemporary pop, rock and country music. Which speaks volumes about their interest in tapping into K-pop’s sunny vibes and fierce fandoms. Republic will collaborate with “Girls Planet” team to promote the band and a global rollout of the group’s debut project.

	“The reason why we are teaming up with Republic collector is to create a girl group targeting the U.S. market directly. So that’s the biggest difference with the previous season,” Kim Sinyoung told Variety.
	

	Mnet’s “Planet’ music competition has traveled beyond Korea as a success in Thailand and Japan, among other markets. In Japan it airs on the popular free streaming platform Abema.

	Kim Sinyoung said he has learned key truths about talent and stardom by through his work on the “Planet” series. Musical talent is essential, he observed, but it’s only one element that an artist aka “idols” in the slanguage of K-pop) needs to ascend to true stardom.

	“Skills like singing and dancing are very important [to win] this talent show. But more important are a strong character and personality to grab the attention of the audiences,” Kim Sinyoung said. “So we are now really trying to figure out when we do the auditions — we are trying to see their character, not only the skills like a singing and dancing.”



	

					Two judges who screened walk-up auditions for the K-pop talent competition series “Girls Planet” during the KCON Korean culture festival in downtown Los Angeles. (Variety/Cynthia Littleton)
	



	The show plans to hold ore auditions later this year in New York and London, and Kim Sinyoung also plans to return to Los Angeles for a talent scouting trip. Through a translator, Kim Sinyoung reinforced the qualities that he will look for in selecting “Girls Planet” contestants.

	“He’s looking for something that makes audience fall in love with the applicants,” he said. “There could be a lot of things that people like to get into someone. It could be their skill sets are like super talented, or someone has their own like personal history, or just their character or their charm. That’s what he’s looking for.”

	Like its predecessors, “Girls Planet” will begin with a field of 100 contestants that will be winnowed to about 20. CJ ENM press reps emphasized that there’s been no decision yet on the number of members in the “Girls Planet’ creation.
	

	The series in the past has typically spanned 10-12 episodes per season that run on a weekly basis. The finale episode airs live, much like ABC’s “American Idol” and NBC’s “The Voice.” The “Planet” series finales have a compelling horserace aspect because the public votes are tallied live, Kim Sinyoung said. Previous seasons of the show have been determined by the votes of more than 7 million viewers.

	“It gives the feeling of watching the presidential election — like a vote count,” Kim Sinyoung said.

	The “Planet” series has a solid track record of launching K-pop acts in recent years. Kim Sinyoung is grateful that he was able to parlay his childhood love of MTV and music competition TV shows into a career as a producer. During his college years Kim Sinyoung studied in New York (“Where I really loved to see Variety magazine,” he noted) before returning to Korea to work his way up in the competitive arena of music-related TV. As such, he’s been perfectly positioned to see the impact on the nation from the explosive global growth of K-pop, Korean movies and TV, beauty products, food and cultural exports (which include “K-pop Demon Hunters”).

	Kim Sinyoung attended the first KCON gathering in Los Angeles, more than 10 years ago. The event was significantly smaller in size and scope back then.

	“At the time, there were not many audiences like this,” he said, gesturing to the crowds of fans gathering in clusters inside the L.A. Convention Center. “So it’s very surprising to see this much of a crowd here lining up” to audition for “Girls Planet, he said. “I’m very happy to see that.”

schema.headline: Producers Scout for K-pop Talent With U.S. Appeal During KCON Fan Festival in Los Angeles

title: ‘Club Kid’ Trailer: Jordan Firstman Is a Party Promoter With a Surprise Son in His A24 Cannes Sensation
description: After making a splash at this year’s Cannes Film Festival — and sparking a studio bidding war that culminated in a $17 million sale from A24 — Jorda
body:
After making a splash at this year’s Cannes Film Festival — and sparking a studio bidding war that culminated in a $17 million sale from A24 — Jordan Firstman‘s film “Club Kid” has its first trailer.

	Firstman wrote and directed the film, which stars Cara Delevingne, Diego Calva, Kirby Howell-Baptiste and Reggie Absolom. It follows a queer party promoter, played by Firstman, who has long outgrown his time on the scene. However, his life is upended when he suddenly meets the 10-year-old son he never knew he had, leading him to grapple with the kind of life he wants to lead.
	

	In his review out of Cannes, Variety film critic Guy Lodge wrote that “Club Kid” is a “sweet, surprisingly old-fashioned heartwarmer,” noting that the film’s opening sequence evokes the style of “Anora” director Sean Baker.


	Firstman, who previously appeared in “I Love LA,” “English Teacher,” “Hacks” and “Rotting in the Sun,” is widely known for his online sketch comedy. At Cannes, sources told Variety that A24, Netflix, Searchlight Pictures, Focus Features and Mubi were the leading contenders hoping to score his sentimental festival favorite. “Club Kid” is poised to be one of A24’s big awards pushes this fall, in addition to Jesse Eisenberg’s “The Debut.”

	After nabbing a distribution deal from A24, Firstman told Variety that honoring his queer cast on the promotional tour was crucial: “In every one of my buyer meetings [it] was vital to me that this cast gets brought out in full to promote the film – flown out, put up, glam paid for, all of it.”

	“Club Kid” releases in theaters on November 6. Watch the trailer below.

schema.headline: ‘Club Kid’ Trailer: Jordan Firstman Is a Party Promoter With a Surprise Son in His A24 Cannes Sensation

title: Yami Gautam Dhar’s ‘Nayyi Navelli’ Sets October Release From Amazon MGM Studios, Colour Yellow (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Amazon MGM Studios and Colour Yellow have set “Nayyi Navelli,” an Indian fantasy family entertainer starring Yami Gautam Dhar, for release in cinema
body:
Amazon MGM Studios and Colour Yellow have set “Nayyi Navelli,” an Indian fantasy family entertainer starring Yami Gautam Dhar, for release in cinemas this October, timed to the Dussehra festival period.

	Balaji Mohan directs from a script by Himanshu Sharma and Divy Nidhi Sharma. Aanand L Rai and Sharma produce through Colour Yellow, marking the banner’s first collaboration with Amazon MGM Studios. G.V. Prakash Kumar composes the music.
	

	The story follows a new bride whose arrival turns a turbulent household in Meerut into a picture of domestic harmony, until her brother-in-law grows convinced that his seemingly perfect sister-in-law is secretly a “daayan,” or witch. The film is billed as a blend of family comedy and fantasy adventure built around festive theatrical viewing.


	Nikhil Madhok, director and head of SVOD Originals at Prime Video India and Amazon MGM Studios, called the project a natural fit for the holiday. “As we saw ‘Nayyi Navelli’ finally come together, there was an instant, collective realization that this is THE Dussehra film. No other date would do it justice,” Madhok said. He added that Gautam Dhar and the supporting cast delivered strong performances, and that the studio, working alongside Colour Yellow, expects the film to be a top choice for family audiences during the holiday.

	Rai described the project as one built on surprise. “‘Nayyi Navelli’ is the kind of story that surprises you at every turn,” he said, noting that he and Sharma were drawn to how the script folds fantasy, comedy and adventure into a story about family. Rai said Gautam Dhar was an obvious fit for the role, bringing both warmth and mischief to the part, and that he is looking forward to the studio’s first project with Amazon MGM Studios reaching audiences.
	

	Colour Yellow, founded by Rai, has built its slate around original stories with strong character work, including “Raanjhanaa,” “Tanu Weds Manu,” “Tere Ishk Mein,” “Tumbbad” and “Tu Yaa Main.” Yami Gautam Dhar’s most recent role was a cameo in blockbuster “Dhurandhar: The Revenge,” and she headlined “Haq” and “Article 370.”

	“Nayyi Navelli” opens in cinemas on Oct. 16.

schema.headline: Yami Gautam Dhar’s ‘Nayyi Navelli’ Sets October Release From Amazon MGM Studios, Colour Yellow (EXCLUSIVE)

title: The Beatles Ink Licensing and Merch Deal With Universal Music Ahead of Biopics
description: The Beatles‘ rights-holding company Apple Corps has come together with Universal Music Group to ink a wide-ranging licensing and merch deal for all
body:
The Beatles‘ rights-holding company Apple Corps has come together with Universal Music Group to ink a wide-ranging licensing and merch deal for all things related to the fab four.

	It will include physical and digital merchandise, licensing and e-commerce. “The Beatles embody music’s power to change the world, and that influence makes them one of the most iconic and enduring cultural brands of all time,” said Lucian Grainge, chairman and CEO of Universal Music Group. “We’re grateful for Apple Corps’ trust as we deepen our global partnership, while protecting and growing the Beatles’ legacy through authentic fan experiences worthy of their artistry. As a lifelong Beatles fan, building on the relationships forged over the past 14 years is one of the great highlights of my career.”
	

	The worldwide exclusive pact comes ahead of the highly-anticipated quartet of Sam Mendes biopics about the group, in which Paul Mescal will play Paul McCartney, Harris Dickinson portrays John Lennon, Joseph Quinn stars as George Harrison and Barry Keoghan is Ringo Starr. Titled “The Beatles – A Four Film Cinematic Event,” the four-movie project is currently in production and set to be released in 2028.


	Apple Corps – unrelated to the Steve Jobs-founded tech company – was formed in 1968 to oversee the Beatles’ creative and business interests. The entity has embarked on a vigorous program of experiences and other projects to introduce the legendary band to a new generation of fans. Chief among them is an upcoming immersive experience in London, due to launch in 2027, which will feature seven floors of archival material as well as a store selling merchandise and a recreation of the studio where “Let it Be” was recorded. The building, on 3 Savile Row, is where the group played an unforgettable rooftop concert and fans will have an opportunity to relive the experience on the spot it took place.
	

	“We are delighted to partner with UMG on a new global merchandising deal,” said Tom Greene, CEO of Apple Corps. “There has never been a more exciting time to work on the Beatles as we look ahead to the 3 Saville Row fan experience in 2027, and our biopic movies in 2028. The Beatles’ message has never been more relevant or needed in the world today, and we look forward to delighting millions of fans with everything we have planned.”

schema.headline: The Beatles Ink Licensing and Merch Deal With Universal Music Ahead of Biopics

title: Hamaguchi Ryusuke, Pawel Pawlikowski Cannes Winners Among El Gouna’s First 10 Titles for Ninth Edition
description: El Gouna Film Festival has revealed the first 10 titles for its ninth edition, set to run Oct. 15-23, in the Red Sea resort town of El Gouna, Egypt.
body:
El Gouna Film Festival has revealed the first 10 titles for its ninth edition, set to run Oct. 15-23, in the Red Sea resort town of El Gouna, Egypt.

	The lineup spans work from established auteurs and first-time feature directors, drawing from festivals including Cannes, Berlin, Sundance and Karlovy Vary.

	Among the titles is Hamaguchi Ryusuke‘s “All of a Sudden,” a French-Japanese-German-Belgian co-production starring Virginie Efira as a nursing home director in the Parisian suburbs who introduces a humane care method against resistance, and whose life shifts after meeting a terminally ill Japanese playwright played by Okamoto Tao. The film earned a best actress prize for Efira and Okamoto at Cannes.
	

	Pawel Pawlikowski, the director behind “Ida” and “Cold War,” is in the selection with “Fatherland,” a German-Polish-Italian-French production starring Sandra Hüller and Hanns Zischler as Erika and Thomas Mann on a road trip through post-war Europe. The film won a shared best director prize at Cannes.


	Also in the selection is “American Doctor,” from Poh Si Teng, following three American doctors of different backgrounds who enter Gaza to save lives and find themselves risking everything to expose the truth. Teng previously produced the Oscar-nominated “St. Louis Superman” and served as an Emmy-winning executive producer on “Patrice: The Movie.” The film premiered at Sundance and won the Amnesty International Award and the Peter Wintonick Audience Award at the Thessaloniki International Documentary Festival.

	Joaquín del Paso’s “The Garden We Dreamed” follows a Haitian family that settles in a Mexican forest shaped by illegal logging, finding fragile moments of love and resilience. The film screened at the Berlinale and won the Golden Biznaga for best Ibero-American film, along with Silver Biznaga honors for best director and cinematography at the Málaga International Film Festival.
	

	Mads Mengel’s feature debut “The Guest” centers on new parents whose plans to announce their baby’s name are upended when the father’s estranged mother arrives unannounced. The Danish film took the best director prize and a special jury award at Karlovy Vary.

	Myrsini Aristidou’s debut feature “Hold Onto Me” follows an 11-year-old girl who tracks down and slowly bonds with the estranged father she barely knows. The Cyprus-Denmark-Greece co-production won the audience award in the World Cinema Dramatic category at Sundance.

	Juliette Binoche stars in Lance Hammer’s “Queen at Sea,” a U.K.-U.S. production about a family pushed to its breaking point as a mother’s advancing dementia raises the question of who decides what is best for her. The film won the Silver Bear Jury Prize at the Berlinale, along with a Silver Bear for best supporting performance shared by Tom Courtenay and Anna Calder-Marshall.

	Markus Schleinzer’s “Rose,” Austria’s submission for best international feature at the 2027 Academy Awards, follows a stranger who talks his way into a war-shattered village as its new farmer while concealing an audacious deception. Sandra Hüller won a Silver Bear for best leading performance for the role at the Berlinale.

	“Who Killed Alex Odeh?,” directed by William Lafi Youmans and Jason Osder, revisits the unsolved bombing that killed Palestinian American community leader Alex Odeh four decades ago, as a journalist reopens the cold case and uncovers buried records. The documentary won the Jury Award for Journalistic Excellence and the Producers Award for Nonfiction at Sundance.

	Rounding out the initial selection is İlker Çatak’s “Yellow Letters,” a German-French production in which a celebrated artist couple’s marriage is tested after an incident at their play’s premiere draws the attention of the state. The film won the Golden Bear at the Berlinale.

	El Gouna artistic director Andrew Mohsen said: “These 10 films speak to each other in unexpected ways, through family, identity, and the quiet acts of courage it takes to hold onto both or to pursue the truth. That’s what El Gouna has always been about, bringing stories from all over the world into the same room, connecting audiences and filmmakers.”

	Further additions to the program will be revealed in the coming weeks.

schema.headline: Hamaguchi Ryusuke, Pawel Pawlikowski Cannes Winners Among El Gouna’s First 10 Titles for Ninth Edition

title: Emily Watson Says Growing Up in a Religious Cult Almost Stopped Her From Starring in ‘Breaking the Waves’: ‘I Was Like a Piece of Wire That Had Been Unplugged’
description: Emily Watson is one of the most lauded actors working today, having earned multiple Oscar, Golden Globe and BAFTA nominations, as well as winning a
body:
Emily Watson is one of the most lauded actors working today, having earned multiple Oscar, Golden Globe and BAFTA nominations, as well as winning a Silver Bear in Berlin, a European Film Award and a SAG Award. But growing up in a religious cult almost ended her illustrious career before it even began. 

	Speaking at the Sarajevo Film Festival, where she is presiding over the jury as well as receiving an honorary Heart of Sarajevo Award, the “Chernobyl” star spoke candidly about the experience of growing up as part of the School of Philosophy and Economic Science. The London-based organization advocates for conservative values, with strictly traditional gender roles and sexual ethics, and has often been described by former members as a sect, new religious movement, and a cult, with Watson describing it as the latter.  
	

	“Parts of it were very happy, and parts of it were very strange,” she recalled. “I think a lot of artists have themes in their childhood that they have to overcome. I was born into a very lovely family, but I grew up in a kind of religious cult that was very strict. I was a very devotional young person. I felt very strongly about it. It took me a while to find my way because of that.”


	Watson credits acting with “saving her life.” While she began her performing career on stage as part of the Royal Shakespeare Company, it was Lars von Trier’s “Breaking the Waves” that sent the actor into international prominence. The 1996 drama saw Watson play Bess McNeill, a young woman living in a repressed, deeply religious community in the north of Scotland. There, she falls in love with a Danish oil worker played by Stellan Skarsgård. When he suffers a life-altering accident, Watson embarks on a sexual journey that contradicts the strict moral guidelines of her community.
	

	When “Breaking the Waves” premiered at the Cannes Film Festival in 1996, Watson’s religious upbringing was not widely known. According to the actor, it took her a “lifetime” to process her childhood, but she can now see the stark parallels between her personal life and the breakout role that landed her a first Oscar nomination. 

	“I did know that I had an affinity with this character,” she said of Bess. “There is an interesting part to this story that, when I told the people at the School of Economic Science that I was going to do a film and they inquired as to the nature of it, I was summoned and told in no uncertain terms that I was not to do this. I was told to go on my undignified way.”

	“That moment was a rupture,” she went on. “This is where I’d grown up, where my friends were, and I walked away. I was desperately upset, but I also had a sense that my heart was taking flight. An incredible freedom. I knew in that moment that I should trust that feeling, because my true inner self sent me on the right path. But that sense of rupture, when there’s a sort of a nuclear explosion and an exposure to light and energy… All of that is in the movie. That’s part of why it works, because I was like a piece of wire being unplugged.” 



	

					“Breaking the Waves,” courtesy of Zentropa
	



	Still, despite this cataclysmic synergy between art and real life, Watson did not tell Skarsgård about her upbringing until 2016, when they shared the screen again in the hit show “Chernobyl.” “He literally did a spit take,” she recalled. “It felt so private at the time [of shooting the film]. I didn’t understand what was happening to me.” 

	Watson has become more comfortable and open about talking about her past in the last decade, which she credits to a wide “societal understanding” of how it is “healthy to explore the damage that happens in your childhood.” “In the early 1990s, that wasn’t a thing in the way that it is now. It has taken me a lifetime to unpick it all. I wouldn’t have been able to articulate any of this [in 1996]. I was very defensive.” 

	That defensiveness, she said, was also very visible during her time at Cannes with “Breaking the Waves.” Recalling the overwhelming experience of doing a press conference at the French fete, Watson said she now realizes how “reserved” she came across as. The high-pressure environment had the young performer closing up, with Watson recalling how all she could think about was wanting to “come off as the most normal, boring person in the world, because to let anybody in, to let anybody know anything about me, isn’t safe.” 
	

	Her parents, who were still attached to the religious group, went with their daughter to the festival. “It was sort of uncomfortable because they, on one hand, supported me and were very lovely about it,” she said. “My dad, coming out of this screening, was the color of this [white] dress. Any father watching that film would have that reaction. But at the same time they didn’t speak on my behalf in the organization, so it was a very complex situation. But we matured, we communicated, and we were good.”

	Being on the Oscar trail for both “Breaking the Waves” and Anand Tucker’s “Hilary and Jackie” was equally overwhelming, but Watson recognizes that awards campaigns have become “much more extreme” in the years since. “The commercial nature of it is sad because it is not a true meritocracy. It’s about money, which makes a festival like this so beautiful. It’s very pure and lovely swimming in the river of storytelling here.”

	Elsewhere in the conversation, Watson spoke about wanting to work with more female directors, despite not having done so often throughout her career. “That’s not me, that’s the industry,” she emphasized. “There are obviously a lot of brilliant female [directors]. But the fight to get to that level is a lot easier for men.” She noted how “incredible” the experience was of working with Chloe Zhao on “Hamnet.” “She takes you on a spiritual journey and makes the movie about it.” 

	Asked by a Palestinian audience member about the difficulties that marginalized actors have in entering a highly competitive industry, particularly those who work in war-torn countries, Watson said it is an “imaginative leap” for her to imagine how hard that must be. “What I do say to everybody is that Shakespeare belongs to Palestine as much as everywhere else.” 

	The actor recalled watching Michael Winterbottom’s “Welcome to Sarajevo” the night prior and realizing how “storytelling advocating for a place or people is so powerful.” “We are all in that river of creativity. I totally understand that resources are very sparse. I think a camera is a camera is a camera, and if you are open, it can see you.”

	As for what is next for Watson, the actor is set to appear on the second season of HBO Max’s “Dune: Prophecy,” as well as star in Mira Nair’s historical drama “AMRI.” She also told Screen International during Sarajevo that she will appear in Mackenzie Crook’s directorial debut, “Mars Express,” alongside Toby Jones. The film tells the real-life story of Colin and Judith Pillinger and their mission to find life on Mars in the late 1990s.

schema.headline: Emily Watson Says Growing Up in a Religious Cult Almost Stopped Her From Starring in ‘Breaking the Waves’: ‘I Was Like a Piece of Wire That Had Been Unplugged’

title: San Sebastián Sets Fatih Akin’s ‘Ghost Song’ as Opening Night Film
description: “Ghost Song” (“Geister”), from multi-prized German auteur Fatih Akin (“In the Fade”), has been set as the opening night film at this year’s San Seba
body:
“Ghost Song” (“Geister”), from multi-prized German auteur Fatih Akin (“In the Fade”), has been set as the opening night film at this year’s San Sebastián Film Festival.

	A world premiere, “Ghost Song” is hailed by the San Sebastián Festival as “a poetic drama about loss and longing.” It will bow at San Sebastián on Sept. 18, playing in main competition, after a opening gala where Werner Herzog will accept a San Sebastián career achievement Donostia Award, giving San Sebastián’s get-go a strong German accent, after Germany has scored nine productions and coproductions at Locarno, 22 at Venice and 18 at Toronto.
	

	Sold by Beta Cinema and starring Eren M. Güvercin (“Banksters”) and Mariam Dawoud, “Ghost Song” turns on Farasha, 20, who after her death, enters Faris’ dreams, sparking what is described as “a passionate romance that blurs the line between dreams and reality.”


	Akin has called “Ghost Song” “a love story, but not like the Patrick Swayze-Demi Moore film — though maybe it is a mix between the Patrick Swayze-Demi Moore film and Jean-Paul Sartre. It’s a mix of that.”

	The berth marks the latest honor for Akin who broke out with 2004’s “Head-On,” which scooped a Berlin Golden Bear, while The Edge of Heaven (2007) took a Cannes best screenplay, while 2017’s “In the Fade” won best actress at Cannes for Diane Kruger tour de force performance and a Golden Globe in the foreign language film category.

	A career packed by big fest prizes and critical acclaim came to near total halt with Venice competition contender “The Cut,” bog budget ($21 million) tale set about the 1915 Armenian genocide, sparking a more eclectic mid career with a return to form via 2017’s “In the Fade” but also the more experimental neo-horror “The Golden Glove,” and last year’s “Amrun,” inherited from friend and mentor Hark Bohm and a 1945 coming-of-age tale which has proved Akun’s biggest commercial hit of his career in Germany, helping to sae his production company, he has recognised.
	

	Arthouse for teens, as Akin has said, “Ghost Song” looks like another departure though reflecting his resolution “with each film to do it different.”

	As younger audiences replace ageing baby boomers at archaise cinemas in Europe, “Ghost Song” also reflects a marked move toward younger-skewing arthouse, whether a conscious market ploy or not.

	“Ghost Song” is produced by Akin’s label Bombero International and Warner Bros. Film Productions Germany, in co-production with Rialto Film, his partners on “Amrun.”

title: Catherine Zeta-Jones Thriller Series ‘Kill Jackie’ Sets October Release Date on Prime Video
description:
Catherine Zeta-Jones‘ highly anticipated thriller series, “Kill Jackie,” has set a premiere date on Prime Video.

	The Fremantle and Steel Springs P
body:
Catherine Zeta-Jones‘ highly anticipated thriller series, “Kill Jackie,” has set a premiere date on Prime Video.

	The Fremantle and Steel Springs Pictures production will release all eight episodes Oct. 2 on the streamer in the U.K., Ireland, Netherlands, Turkey, Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg and Canada. It will also launch on the same day on AMC+ in the U.S.


	Based on the acclaimed novel “The Price You Pay” by Nick Harkaway, writing as pseudonym Aidan Truhen, “Kill Jackie” stars Zeta-Jones as a former international drug smuggler turned art dealer whose past comes back to haunt her. 
	

	“Just as life starts to feel a little boring, it takes a sudden lethal turn when she discovers that The Seven Demons, a squad of the world’s most terrifying hitmen, have been hired to kill her,” the series’ official synyopsis reads. “Assuming someone from her past is behind it, Jackie unleashes her old instincts and embarks on a wild, dangerous game plan: to take down The Demons one by one before they kill her. However, she soon realizes her own demons are much more terrifying than the ruthless killers on her trail…and her buried secrets lead her closer to home, with surprising consequences.”


	Alongside Zeta-Jones, “Kill Jackie” also stars aniel Ings, Sidse Babett Knudsen, Bill Paterson, Ron Perlman, Óscar Jaenada, Hattie Hook, Darci Shaw, Raff Law, Enzo Cilenti, Christine Adams, Julian Rhind-Tutt, Karlis Arnolds Avots, Set Sjöstrand, Tadashi Ito, Sebastian Armesto, Julian Barratt, Gavin Spokes, Jonathan Cake and Bamshad Abedi-Amin.

	“Kill Jackie” is co-produced by Fremantle and Steel Springs Pictures and co-created by “Gangs of London” creatives Conor Keane and Tom Butterworth alongside Peter Lawson (“John Wick”) and Damon Thomas (“Killing Eve”). Thomas is lead directing with Butterworth writing and showrunning. Keane co-wrote the TV adaptation and is also serving as associate producer. Executive producers include Lawson and Jose Agustin Valdes for Steel Springs Pictures as well as Butterworth, Thomas and Zeta-Jones with Rebecca Dundon, Dante Di Loreto and Jeffrey Levine. Harkaway was an executive consultant on the series.

title: ZZ Top Drummer Frank Beard Dead at 77
description:
ZZ Top
                          Frank Beard
                          Dead at 77
body:
ZZ Top
                          Frank Beard
                          Dead at 77
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                August 18, 2026
                
                            11:50 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 18, 2026
                                8:05 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
            Frank Beard, the longtime drummer for legendary rock band ZZ Top, has died ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            According to the Fort Bend County Medical Examiner Frank passed away on August 17 at his Texas ranch with family by his side after a stay in hospice. A cause of death has not been disclosed at this time.
      
    
            ZZ Top founder Billy F. Gibbons released a statement on his passing saying, “Today, Elwood and I lost a great friend and collaborator, and the world lost one of the most naturally innovative drummers and a great and true son of Texas. His signature backbeat was key to keeping ZZ on top. The band of which he was part for six decades is going to keep on keeping on as he had wished.”
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported ... Frank's health forced ZZ Top to cancel its August 5 concert at the Hollywood Bowl.
      

            With the passing of Frank, ZZ Top is canceling their show tonight in Salt Lake City and tomorrow Colorado Springs ... they'll resume this weekend with two dates at Austin City Limits -- at one of Frank's favorite venues.
      
    
            Frontman Billy Gibbons said at the time the band was dealing with "insurmountable obstacles" and asked fans to bear with them during the interruption.
      
    
            Frank had also been absent from the band's recent performances ... with drummer Michael Monahan filling in behind the kit. ZZ Top performed without Frank in Saratoga, California just days before TMZ learned of his death.
      
    
            Frank joined ZZ Top in 1969 ... spending more than five decades anchoring the group alongside Gibbons and late bassist Dusty Hill.
      
    
            He played on all 15 of the band's studio albums and helped power some of its biggest hits, including "La Grange," "Tush," "Gimme All Your Lovin’," "Sharp Dressed Man" and "Legs."
      
    
        
                    
                      12/5/12
                  
      
    
            ZZ Top was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2004. The group's classic lineup remained intact until Dusty died in 2021.
      
    
            Frank was 77.
      
    
            RIP
